**Claim.** Yes — for a general composition of an IND-CPA encryption scheme and a (S)UF-CMA MAC, Encrypt-then-MAC is the provably safe ordering; MAC-then-Encrypt (and Encrypt-and-MAC) are not secure in general.

**Setup/Assumptions.**
- Enc = (Gen, Enc, Dec), randomized, IND-CPA secure; decryption may be an arbitrary deterministic algorithm (no "benign" behavior assumption).
- Mac = (Gen, Sign, Ver), SUF-CMA (strong unforgeability: can't produce a valid tag for any pair (m, σ) not previously returned by the oracle, even if m was previously MAC'd with a different tag). Note: with randomized Enc, EtM can be shown under EUF-CMA; SUF-CMA is the clean standard assumption (Bellare–Nampremre 2000).
- Keys independent (K_e ≠ K_m).
- Security goal for composition: authenticated encryption, i.e., IND-CCA privacy (+ ciphertext integrity).

**Why EtM works.** Ciphertext = (c, t) where c = Enc(Ke, m; r) and t = MAC(Km, c) [the IV/randomness is included in c]. On decryption, verify t against c before decrypting. Reduction: any CCA adversary A that gets plaintext from the decryption oracle must submit a ciphertext that passes verification. The transcript of A's encryption queries gives MAC queries only on ciphertexts Enc produced; since Enc is randomized, all accepted ciphertexts are fresh for the MAC with overwhelming probability, so passing verification implies a MAC forgery → contradicts SUF-CMA. Hence the decryption oracle is useless and privacy reduces to IND-CPA. Bonus: integrity of ciphertext (INT-CTXT) comes for free.

**Why MtE is not safe in general.** Ciphertext = Enc(Ke, m || MAC(Km, m)). Verification requires decrypting first: any decryption oracle (or any observable difference in how the receiver fails — padding errors vs MAC errors, timing, error messages) is exposed before authentication. Two kinds of attacks:
1. Concrete/real-world: CBC + PKCS padding (SSL/TLS, SSH). The receiver decrypts, strips padding, then checks MAC. Vaudenay's padding oracle recovers plaintext in ~128·2^8 probes per block; timing variants (Lucky Thirteen) and POODLE exploited exactly this ordering. The primitives (AES-CBC is IND-CPA, HMAC is EUF-CMA) were each secure — the composition broke them.
2. Generic counterexample (shows no reduction is possible): take any IND-CPA Enc and redefine Dec' to leak one bit of the plaintext on the error string whenever the MAC check fails (or always). Dec' is still IND-CPA (CPA adversaries never see Dec'), and any SUF-CMA MAC remains so. In MtE, the decryption oracle has to run Dec' before it can check the MAC, so the oracle leaks plaintext bits → IND-CCA of the composition is broken. Hence MtE security can only be shown for specific instantiations case-by-case, never generically.

**Why not E&M either** (briefly): MAC on plaintext can leak plaintext info (e.g., equality), and generic IND-CCA fails for similar reasons; SSH works because of specific instantiations + countermeasures.

**Conclusion.** EtM is preferred: MAC verification gates decryption, the proof needs only standard assumptions, and it is what modern AEADs (GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) do internally — MAC over ciphertext.

**Streaming:** Fixed 64 KiB plaintext chunks, constant memory; u32 length-prefixed ciphertext chunks; final chunk tagged FINAL; decryption requires FINAL on the last chunk and exact plaintext length match (from the header) → detects truncation.

**Single most likely pitfall:** Forgetting to authenticate the file header (not passing the header as associated data). Everything before the first ciphertext chunk — salt, Argon2id parameters, the secretstream header — sits unauthenticated in the file; an attacker can downgrade opslimit/memlimit (cheapening offline brute force) or transplant headers across files. Runner-up: nonce/key reuse via deterministic derivation (e.g., deriving the key without a fresh salt, or reusing a header with the same key).
